extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent applicants/patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on determining whether a claimed invention meets the statutory utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. 101 (and related 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement/support issues), including standards for asserted utilities, well-established utilities, evidentiary burdens, and handling replies and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of dependent claims follows independent claim (same statutory class)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim is treated as defining an invention that has utility if the independent claim from which the dependent claim depends is drawn to the same statutory class of invention as the dependent claim and the independent claim defines an invention having utility. An exception exists where the utility specified for the invention defined in a dependent claim differs from that indicated for the invention defined in the independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant has established utility for a species within a claimed genus and presents a generic claim covering the genus, as a general matter that claim should be treated as sufficient under 35 U.S.C. 101 unless it can be established that other species clearly encompassed by the claim do not have utility. In such cases encourage amendment to exclude non-usable species.

rubrics_metrics.name: One credible assertion of specific utility suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not 'credible', do not render the claimed invention lacking in utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Raytheon v. Roper; In re Gottlieb; In re Malachowski. If applicant makes one credible assertion, utility for the claimed invention as a whole is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant statements alone cannot, standing alone, support lack-of-utility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or incident to prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack of utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office should not require removal of nonessential statements relating to utility from a disclosure regardless of technical accuracy. Be careful not to read unclaimed results, limitations, or embodiments into a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect asserted or well-established utility on initial examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon initial examination, the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are any statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose. A complete disclosure should include a statement identifying a specific and substantial utility for the invention unless the invention has a well-established utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no statements found, determine if the claimed invention has a 'well-established utility' (see separate criterion). If not, proceed with rejection procedure and inform applicant to indicate why invention is useful and where support exists in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asserted utility must be specific and substantial
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant believes the invention is useful and must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the claimed invention is useful. Vague assertions (e.g., 'biological activity', 'pharmacological effects') are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of insufficient statements: unspecified 'biological activity' (Brenner v. Manson), disclosure that something is 'plastic-like' or can form 'films' (In re Ziegler), or mere 'biologically active'. A proper statement usually explains the purpose or how the invention may be used (e.g., useful in treating a particular disorder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-established utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has a well-established utility if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on the characteristics of the invention, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If well-established, rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should not be imposed even if the specification omits a statement of specific and substantial utility (example: cloning of insulin sequence).

rubrics_metrics.name: If no asserted or well-established utility, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112
rubrics_metrics.description: If no statement asserting a specific and substantial utility exists in the specification and the invention lacks a well-established utility, the examiner should reject the application under 35 U.S.C. 101 and under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) as failing to identify a specific and substantial utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection should clearly indicate that the basis is failure to identify a specific and substantial utility and specify that applicant must reply indicating why the invention is useful and where support can be found in the specification as filed. See MPEP § 2701 for reply handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of utility from applicant's assertion (Langer test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's assertion of utility creates a presumption of utility that will usually be sufficient to satisfy the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101. The Office must presume a statement of utility to be true unless there is reason to question its objective truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not start by questioning truth; instead ask if there is reason to question the statement, evaluate the logic and any applicant-cited evidence. See In re Langer and subsequent cases adopting the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility standard for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An asserted utility is credible (believable to a person of ordinary skill based on totality of evidence) unless (A) the logic underlying the assertion is seriously flawed, or (B) the facts upon which the assertion is based are inconsistent with that logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not label inventions 'incredible' or 'speculative' as a starting point. 'Incredible utility' is a conclusion reached only after evaluation of the applicant's assertion and evidentiary basis. Special care for therapeutic utilities (see §2107.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: When asserted utility is not credible (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions have been found not credible where the asserted utility could only be true if it violated a scientific principle or was wholly inconsistent with contemporary knowledge in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include claims that would contravene laws of nature (e.g., second law of thermodynamics) or make claims inconsistent with current scientific knowledge (In re Gazave).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial burden on the Office to make a prima facie case with evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly reject under 35 U.S.C. 101, the Office must (A) make a prima facie showing that the claimed invention lacks utility, and (B) provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in establishing the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must do more than merely question operability; set forth factual reasons that would lead one skilled in the art to question the statement of operability. If the Office cannot develop a proper prima facie case, rejection should not be imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard: preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 is a question of fact and the evidentiary standard used during ex parte examination is a preponderance of the totality of the evidence under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must present countervailing facts and reasoning sufficient to establish that a person of ordinary skill would not believe the applicant’s assertion. Preponderance means 'more likely than not'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing elements when asserted utility is not specific/substantial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted utility is not specific or substantial, a prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not that a person of ordinary skill would not consider any asserted utility specific and substantial. The showing must contain: (A) an explanation of the reasoning, (B) support for factual findings, and (C) evaluation of all relevant evidence including utilities in the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a well-reasoned statement and documentary evidence where possible (journals, treatises, patents); if documentary evidence not available, explain scientific basis for examiner's factual conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing elements when asserted utility is not credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible, a prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not that a person skilled in the art would not consider any asserted utility credible. The showing must include: (A) explanation of the reasoning, (B) support for factual findings, (C) evaluation of all relevant evidence including the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same rigor as for non-specific utilities; articulate reasoning and cite evidence that would lead a skilled person to doubt the assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing when no utility asserted
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no specific and substantial utility is disclosed or well-established, a prima facie showing of no specific and substantial utility need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that, on the record before the examiner, there is no known well-established utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific in setting forth initial rejection so applicant can identify and address assumptions made by the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity required in rejection wording and use of form paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 based on lack of utility must include a detailed explanation why the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility. The MPEP provides form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05.02–7.05.04) and formats A/B/C for different scenarios (no asserted utility; not specific and substantial; not credible; multiple utilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Format A/B/C as appropriate: insert claim numbers and words like 'specific and substantial' or 'credible' per guidance; for multiple utilities address each utility. Where enablement issues also exist, make separate 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections using Wands factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for evidentiary support by examiner should be rare and justified
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate situations the Office may require an applicant to substantiate an asserted utility (e.g., when operativeness would be deemed unlikely by one skilled in the art). However, requests for additional evidence should be imposed rarely and only if necessary to support scientific credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asking for evidence, indicate why the factual record is defective and, where appropriate, what type of evidentiary showing can remedy the problem. The Office must first provide evidence showing that one of ordinary skill would reasonably doubt the asserted utility before shifting the burden to applicant (In re Brana).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher applicant evidentiary burden when asserted utility is incredible or misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged utility appears to be incredible in view of the knowledge of the art, or factually misleading, applicant must establish the asserted utility by acceptable proof; courts have approved higher burdens on applicant in such situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Citron (claims of cure for cancer without clinical data). Examiner should require sufficient evidence of operativeness and explain the evidentiary deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: How applicant may rebut a prima facie rejection for lack of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proper prima facie rejection is imposed, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut. Rebuttal may be by claim amendments, arguments/reasoning, or new evidence submitted in an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 or by a printed publication. New evidence must be relevant to issues raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations that merely express conclusions without establishing a nexus to supporting evidence have limited probative value (In re Grunwell; In re Buchner). Examiners must fully consider and respond to each substantive element of applicant's response and only maintain rejection if totality shows utility not specific, substantial, and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable correlation between evidence and asserted utility is sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence required; evidence will be sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill to conclude that the asserted utility is more likely than not true. A reasonable correlation between the evidence (e.g., biological activity) and the asserted utility is adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant does not need to prove utility beyond a reasonable doubt or with statistical certainty. Data from animal testing or statistically relevant data, arguments, or documentary evidence can establish reasonable correlation (Nelson v. Bowler; Rey-Bellet v. Englehardt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity to compounds with established utility supports therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of structural similarity to a compound known to have a particular therapeutic or pharmacological utility can support an assertion of therapeutic utility for a new compound, particularly when combined with activity data in customary screening animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the existence of structural relationship and the reasoning explaining why that similarity is relevant to the asserted utility. Example: In re Jolles (daunorubicin/doxorubicin relationship).

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro or animal testing is generally sufficient for therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Data from in vitro or animal testing is generally sufficient to support therapeutic utility when there is a reasonable evidentiary correlation between the activity observed and the asserted human therapeutic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have accepted animal model data as satisfactory correlation when predictive of human response. Applicant need not provide actual evidence of success in treating humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should provide documentary evidence when possible to support prima facie showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, examiners should provide documentary evidence (scientific/technical journals, treatises, patents) to support factual basis for a prima facie showing of no specific and substantial credible utility. If documentary evidence is not available, explain the scientific basis for conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use documentary citations regardless of publication date. If relying on factual conclusions without documentary support, provide a clear scientific explanation for the factual conclusions to permit applicant to respond effectively.
